entry: Concentration of awareness directed at a task or phenomenon while mostly excluding others. In [[Cognitive psychology|cognitive psychology]], attention is often described as the allocation of limited processing resources to a subset of information, thoughts, or tasks. It is an umbrella term for several processes, including selective attention (prioritizing some stimuli over others), sustained attention (maintaining focus), divided attention (sharing resources across tasks), and orienting (shifting focus in space or time). Attention is closely linked to working memory, executive functions, and [[Consciousness|consciousness]]. [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz]] emphasized involuntary attention while also recognizing voluntary, directed attention. [[Wilhelm Wundt]] introduced its systematic study into psychology, and [[Hermann von Helmholtz]] showed that one can focus on one stimulus while still perceiving others.

Neurodevelopmental disorder marked by inattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity, and emotional dysregulation that are excessive, pervasive, and developmentally inappropriate. Its symptoms arise from executive dysfunction and can impair professional performance and relationships, predisposing to a diminished quality of life and reduced life expectancy. It is associated with other [[Mental disorder|mental disorders]]. Under the DSM-5, symptoms must be present for six months or more, with at least six symptoms of inattention or hyperactivity/impulsivity for those under 17 and at least five for those 17 or older. The disorder is primarily genetic, with a heritability rate of 70–80%. Treatment is most effective with medication, primarily [[Stimulant|stimulants]] such as [[Methylphenidate]] or [[Amphetamine|amphetamines]], often combined with [[Psychotherapy]]; exercise and dietary modifications have no proven benefit.

Hunnic ruler (r. 434–453) of an empire that also included Ostrogoths, Alans, and Gepids. Attila, also called The Scourge of God, ruled jointly with his elder brother Bleda from 435 until Bleda's death in 445. He crossed the [[Danube]] twice and plundered the [[Balkans]], but was unable to take [[Constantinople]]. He attempted to conquer [[Gaul]], crossing the [[Rhine]] in 451 before being stopped at the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains. He then invaded Italy, devastating the northern provinces, but was unable to take [[Rome]]. After his death, his adviser Ardaric of the Gepids led a successful revolt, and the Hunnic Empire quickly collapsed. Attila lived on as a character in Germanic heroic legend.

Island in the Near Islands group of the [[Aleutian Islands]], [[Alaska]]. It is one of the westernmost points of the state and became uninhabited in 2010, when its Coast Guard LORAN station closed, making it the largest uninhabited island in the United States. It covers 344.7 square miles (893 sq km). The Battle of Attu, in 1943, was the only [[World War II]] land battle fought in territory that is now part of a U.S. state.

City on the [[North Island]] of [[New Zealand]], the country's largest (urban pop., June 2025: approximately 1,547,200). It lies on a narrow [[Isthmus|isthmus]] between two harbors and is one of the few cities with a harbor on each of two major bodies of water. The isthmus was first settled c. 1350. After a British colony was established in 1840, William Hobson chose Auckland as capital; in 1865 the capital moved to [[Wellington]], but the city continued to grow as a port and manufacturing center. Its central business district is New Zealand's leading economic hub. In 2023, 43% of its residents were born overseas. The University of Auckland, founded in 1883, is the largest university in New Zealand.

German automotive manufacturer of luxury vehicles, headquartered in Ingolstadt, [[Bavaria]]. A wholly owned subsidiary of the [[Volkswagen]] Group, it takes its name from the [[Latin]] translation of its founder's surname, Horch, meaning "listen." The four rings of its logo represent the four companies that formed Auto Union in 1932, its predecessor. Volkswagen relaunched the brand with the 1965 introduction of the Audi F103 series.

American soldier and actor, widely celebrated as the most decorated American combat soldier of [[World War II]]. At age 19, in January 1945, he single-handedly held off a German company for an hour and then led a successful counterattack while wounded, earning the Medal of Honor. After the war he acted mostly in [[Western (genre)|Westerns]] and played himself in *To Hell and Back* (1955). He was also an accomplished songwriter who bred quarter horses.

Group of people who participate in a show or encounter a work of art, literature, theater, music, or [[Video game|video games]]. Audience members participate in different ways: some events invite overt participation, while others allow only modest clapping and criticism. In [[Rhetoric|rhetoric]], an immediate audience is face to face with a speaker, while a mediated audience consumes texts through [[Mass media|mass media]] such as television, radio, or the [[Internet]], and its reception is measured through opinion polls and ratings. Theoretical audiences are imagined to help a speaker compose or practice. Media audience studies are now a recognized part of the curriculum.

Sensory system for [[Hearing|hearing]], comprising the [[Ear|ears]] and the central neural pathways that process [[Sound|sound]]. The outer ear funnels vibrations to the eardrum, and the middle-ear ossicles amplify the vibration pressure roughly 20 times. Outer hair cells in the cochlea amplify traveling wave [[Amplitude|amplitudes]] over 40-fold, and there are three to four times as many outer hair cells as inner hair cells. The basilar membrane is narrowest and stiffest at the cochlear base, where high frequencies are sensed, and widest and least stiff at the apex, where low frequencies are sensed. The cochlear nerve has 30,000+ fibers, each most sensitive to one frequency. The superior olivary complex, in the pons, is the first convergence of signals from both ears and helps determine the direction of sounds. Signals ascend to the [[Brainstem|brainstem]] and then to the [[Cerebral cortex|cerebral cortex]].

British actress and humanitarian, a film and fashion icon. Hepburn rose to stardom in *Roman Holiday* (1953), alongside Gregory Peck, becoming the first actress to win an Academy Award, a Golden Globe, and a BAFTA for the same performance. Later films included *Sabrina* (1954) with [[Humphrey Bogart]], *Funny Face* (1957) with [[Fred Astaire]], *Charade* (1963) opposite [[Cary Grant]], and *My Fair Lady* (1964). She is one of only a few entertainers to have won competitive Academy, Emmy, Grammy, and Tony Awards. She contributed to [[UNICEF]] from 1954 onward and worked in some of the poorest communities of Africa, South America, and Asia. In December 1992 she received the US Presidential Medal of Freedom for her work as a UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador. She died of appendix cancer in Switzerland.

Swedish playwright, novelist, poet, essayist, and painter. Strindberg wrote more than 60 plays and more than 30 works of fiction, autobiography, history, cultural analysis, and politics. His naturalistic dramas, including *The Father* (1887) and *Miss Julie* (1888), responded to [[Émile Zola]]'s call for naturalism in the theater and emphasized the role of heredity and environment. Later plays, such as *A Dream Play* (1902), anticipated [[Expressionism|expressionist]] and [[Surrealism|surrealist]] techniques. In the 1890s he studied the [[Occult|occult]], and after a series of apparent psychotic attacks from 1894 to 1896 he was hospitalized. His novel *The Red Room* (1879) is often described as the first modern Swedish novel. His antifeminist writings, including the pamphlet *Marriage* (1884–1886), provoked controversy.

French philosopher and founder of [[Positivism|positivism]]. He is often regarded as the first philosopher of science in the modern sense, and he coined the term [[Sociology|sociology]], treating it as the crowning achievement of the sciences. His six-volume *Cours de philosophie positive* (1830–1842) set out a hierarchy of the sciences and advocated observational and experimental methods. He held that societies pass through theological, metaphysical, and positive stages. His ideas influenced [[John Stuart Mill]], [[George Eliot]], [[Herbert Spencer]], and [[Émile Durkheim]]. His *Religion of Humanity* presaged the development of secular humanist organizations in the 19th century, and its dogmatic structure and perceived authoritarianism provoked controversy. He may have coined the word [[Altruism|altruism]].

French sculptor, considered a founder of modern sculpture. Rejected three times by the École des Beaux-Arts, he trained at an applied arts school in [[Paris]] and in studios before gaining public attention and commissions in his late 30s. Works such as *The Kiss*, *The Burghers of Calais*, and *Monument to Balzac* are known for boldly expressive physicality, and many were criticized as unfinished or fragmented. *The Gates of Hell* includes a figure later known as *The Thinker*. After his exhibit at the [[World's fair|World's Fair]], wealthy private clients sought his work, and by 1900 he was world-renowned. His students included [[Constantin Brâncuși]], Antoine Bourdelle, and Charles Despiau.

French civil engineer and optical physicist. His research led to near-unanimous acceptance of the wave theory of light, which supplanted [[Isaac Newton|Newton]]'s corpuscular theory from the late 1830s until the end of the 19th century. He gave the first satisfactory explanation of [[Diffraction|diffraction]] by straight edges and, by supposing that light waves are purely transverse, explained [[Polarization (waves)|polarization]]. His stepped [[Lens|lens]] extended the visibility of [[Lighthouse|lighthouses]], saving countless lives at sea. He had a lifelong battle with [[Tuberculosis]], which he succumbed to at age 39, and he received the Rumford Medal of the Royal Society on his deathbed.

French mathematician, engineer, and physicist. One of the first to state and prove rigorously the key theorems of [[Calculus|calculus]], thereby creating [[Real analysis|real analysis]], he also pioneered [[Complex analysis|complex analysis]] and the study of permutation groups in [[Abstract algebra|abstract algebra]]. He contributed to [[Continuum mechanics|continuum mechanics]] and other topics in mathematical physics. According to Hans Freudenthal, more concepts and theorems are named for Cauchy than for any other mathematician. He wrote approximately 800 research articles and five complete textbooks. He refused to swear allegiance to the July Monarchy in 1830 and lived in self-imposed exile until 1838.

Christian theologian and philosopher, bishop of Hippo Regius in North Africa. Drawn first to the [[Manichaeism|Manichaean]] faith and then to Neoplatonism, he converted to Christianity in 386 and was baptized by [[Ambrose|Saint Ambrose]]. He is known as Doctor of Grace for his views on the necessity of unmerited, prevenient grace for salvation and on original sin. In *The City of God* he imagined the Church as a spiritual city distinct from the earthly city, written against the backdrop of the fall of the Western Roman Empire. His *Confessions* is considered the first Western [[Autobiography|autobiography]]. He is recognized as a saint by the [[Catholic Church]] and the [[Eastern Orthodox Church]], and many Protestants regard him as a theological father of the [[Reformation|Protestant Reformation]], an interpretation the Catholic Church disputes.

Chilean army officer and dictator (1973–1990). Pinochet led the army in a coup against President [[Salvador Allende]] on September 11, 1973, and was proclaimed president by the junta in 1974. The military had previously received financial and intelligence support from the [[United States]]. The Chilean government counted at least 3,095 executions and forced disappearances, while other estimates of executions range from 1,200 to 3,200. The regime's economic policies, influenced by the free-market "Chicago Boys," included privatization and [[Neoliberalism|neoliberal]] liberalization; supporters credit them with high growth, while critics point to sharply increased [[Economic inequality|economic inequality]]. A 1988 plebiscite saw 56% vote against his continuation as president. He was arrested in London in 1998 under an international warrant and returned to Chile in 2000 after a legal battle.

Elector of Saxony from 1694 and king of Poland (1697–1706 and 1709–1733). Known for his physical strength and for fathering a very large number of children, with contemporary sources claiming between 360 and 380, he converted to Roman Catholicism to be eligible for election to the throne of the [[Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth]]. As elector he made [[Dresden]] a major cultural center, attracting artists from across Europe and building [[Baroque|baroque]] palaces in Dresden and [[Warsaw]]. He led the Commonwealth in the [[Great Northern War]], which allowed the [[Russian Empire]] to strengthen its influence in Poland. His only legitimate son, Augustus III, became king in 1733.

Family (Alcidae) of seabirds in the order Charadriiformes, found throughout the [[Northern Hemisphere]]. Its 25 extant or recently extinct species in 11 genera include the murres, guillemots, auklets, [[Puffin|puffins]], and murrelets. Apart from the extinct [[Great auk]], all auks can fly, and they are excellent swimmers and divers, although they walk clumsily. Auks resemble [[Penguin|penguins]] in appearance, but they are not closely related; the similarity is an example of moderate convergent evolution. Auks spend most of their adult lives at sea and go ashore to breed. Nearly all species nest in colonies, and auks are monogamous, typically laying a single egg.

Scottish song, a poem by [[Robert Burns]] set to a traditional melody. The text, written in 1788, was based on an older Scottish folk song, and the tune adopted in 1799 is pentatonic. Its title may be translated as "old long since" or "times long past." Traditionally sung to bid farewell to the old year at midnight on [[New Year's Eve]], it is also heard at funerals and graduations, and many branches of the [[Scouting]] movement use it to close jamborees.

Japanese new religious movement and doomsday cult, now known as Aleph. It carried out the 1995 [[Tokyo subway sarin attack]] and was found responsible for the 1994 Matsumoto sarin attack. Its founder, Shoko Asahara, and six followers were executed in 2018 after exhausting their appeals. The group split in 2007 into Aleph and Hikari no Wa. Several countries, including [[Japan]], Russia, Canada, and France, have designated it a terrorist organization.

Burmese politician and independence activist, considered the founder of modern Myanmar. A lifelong anti-imperialist, he studied [[Socialism|socialism]] as a student and helped found the Thakin Society and the People's Revolutionary Party. During the Japanese occupation he served as minister of war in the Japan-backed State of Burma, then switched sides to fight with the Allies. After the war he negotiated independence from Britain in the Aung San–Attlee Agreement and served as premier from 1946 to 1947. He led his party to victory in the 1947 general election, but he and most of his cabinet were assassinated six months before independence. He is considered the founder of the Tatmadaw, the country's armed forces. His daughter was [[Aung San Suu Kyi]].

Burmese politician, diplomat, and author. The daughter of [[Aung San]], she became general secretary of the National League for Democracy in 1988 and was awarded the 1991 Nobel Peace Prize. Her party won 81% of the seats in the 1990 general election, but the military government refused to hand over power, and she was under house arrest for almost 15 of the 21 years from 1989 to 2010. After her party won 86% of the seats in 2015, she served as state counsellor of [[Myanmar]] from 2016 to 2021. Arrested after the 2021 coup, she received a final sentence of 33 years in prison, later reduced to 27; in 2026 the government commuted her sentence to house arrest. The [[United Nations]] and the United States condemned the trials as politically motivated. In 2019 she defended the Myanmar military against genocide allegations before the [[International Court of Justice]].

Mughal emperor (r. 1658–1707). Under his reign the [[Mughal Empire]] reached its greatest extent, covering nearly the entire [[Indian subcontinent]]. After defeating his brother Dara Shikoh at the Battle of Samugarh in May 1658, he imprisoned his father, [[Shah Jahan]], in the Agra Fort. He imposed the Fatawa-i Alamgiri as the empire's principal regulating body, and he is credited with building numerous mosques. Critics argue that his policies against non-Muslims abandoned the pluralism of earlier Mughal emperors. Others argue that he opposed bigotry against Hindus, Sikhs, and Shia Muslims and employed more Hindus in his bureaucracy than his predecessors.

Extinct species of large wild cattle, *Bos primigenius*, the ancestor of domestic cattle. Bulls reached a shoulder height of up to 1.8 m and cows 1.55 m, and horns reached 80 cm in length. It ranged from western Europe and northern Africa to East Asia and the [[Indian subcontinent]] during the [[Pleistocene]], and its range contracted in the [[Holocene]] through habitat loss and hunting. The last confirmed individual died in the Jaktorów forest in Poland in 1627. Domestication during the [[Neolithic Revolution]] in the [[Fertile Crescent]] produced the taurine cattle of Europe, while Indian aurochs gave rise to zebu cattle.
